question: A service stores each user's login session in the memory of the server that handled the login. What breaks when you add a second server behind a load balancer?
options: The second server copies the session from the first one automatically
Nothing, because the browser keeps the whole session
Users sent to the other server look logged out, because that server has no session for them
Only the load balancer slows down
explanation: The session lives only in the first server's memory; servers do not share memory by themselves. The browser holds only a cookie with a session id, not the session. The fix is a shared session store that every server can read.

question: In a service, some requests take 2 seconds and most take 20 ms. Which method usually spreads the work more evenly?
options: Least connections, because a server busy with slow requests has more open connections and gets fewer new ones
Round robin, because every server gets the same number of requests
Sending each user to the same server every time
Choosing the server with the highest number
explanation: Round robin gives every server the same number of requests, not the same amount of work, so slow requests can pile up on one server. Least connections sends new work to the least busy server. When all requests take about the same time, round robin works just as well.

question: A health check only confirms that the server's process is running. Why is that not enough?
options: Process checks use too much memory
A running process cannot answer HTTP
The check would remove healthy servers too often
A server can be running but unable to serve, for example when it cannot reach its database
explanation: A useful health check tests what the server needs to answer a real request, such as its database connection. A process check passes even when every real request would fail.
